findings.title: The statement gives user-facing-uncovered two different triggers
findings.recommendation: The fence glosses `user-facing-uncovered` as 'an end-user-visible call no ratified goal covers' (R-adf-3's wording, and the baseline event table's), but its ledger clause, and the moments table rows at lines 24-25, raise that stop only 'when nothing approved covers the call' / 'with nothing approved to rely on'. A requirement, ruling, resolution or explore decision counts as approved for `relies_on`, so an end-user-visible call that a spec requirement supports but no ratified goal covers, made without asking, gets a ledger entry citing the requirement and no stop under the ledger clause, while the gloss and R-adf-3 say it is a stop. The scenario at line 68 uses the goal wording. G2 at first-run is graded on R-adf-3's six conditions, so following the statement as written can fail G2. The same composed text is in src/core/disciplines.ts:31 and :52 and carried into fourteen bodies, so the fix is to the fence and the module together, with the parity test following.

recommendation_options.label: A
recommendation_options.body: Keep R-adf-3's predicates: reword the ledger clause and table rows 24-25 so each of the two conditions triggers on its own gloss (security: nothing approved to rely on; user-facing: no ratified goal covers), so a user-facing call relying only on a requirement still writes the stop and cites nothing.

recommendation_options.label: B
recommendation_options.body: Read 'approved' as the intended trigger for both, change the user-facing gloss to 'an end-user-visible call nothing approved covers', and take the R-adf-3 rewording to the user at an architect session (a ruling amendment), since the change cannot amend the ruling itself.

findings.title: Upstream-verbatim scenario does not name the reference sync-specs now ships
findings.recommendation: The `Upstream-verbatim — kept unchanged` THEN lists what orbit-sync-specs's `# Orbit additions` carries (the epitome and invocation notes). Since this change, the sync-specs template also declares `references: [decision-records.md]` (src/core/templates/workflows/sync-specs.ts), so the skill now ships a file upstream's never did. Not a violation of the sentence, which speaks of the body, but a cherry-pick reader of the disposition would not learn of it; add a clause naming the decision-record reference the epitome's statement points at.

findings.title: Reference's citation existence rules are looser than the write gate's
findings.recommendation: CITATION_EXISTS says a `goal` is accepted when the doc 'opens a ## Goals item with **<id>' (no whole-ID rule: `G1` does not match `**G10`), and a `resolution` when a record 'exists', omitting that it must read as JSON with `command: resolution` and, for `{doc, token}`, carry that doc. A writer following the reference gets a refusal round-trip rather than a wrong record, so the cost is low; state the whole-match rule and the resolution checks, as `orbit-decision-records`' `A ledger entry names what it relies on` does.

findings.title: Docs do not say the workflows now write decision records on their own
findings.recommendation: docs/cli.md describes `ledger`, `stop` and `resolution` as commands, and docs/ names no execution discipline anywhere. After this change every workflow body tells the AI to write records under every setting, so an adopter upgrading will find `.orbit-runs/decisions/` files appearing in their trail with no page saying why. One sentence in the `orbit emit` section (or the trail description in docs/concepts.md) naming the decision-writing discipline would close it.
